_about: Pave Agent use cases, from Pave's product team mockup (Pave Agent Use Cases, October 20, 2026). One record per use case: the index pages, filters, detail page and related links all build from these. To add one, copy a record and fill every field. Outputs are sample data. [Brackets] in a prompt mark what the reader fills in.

page.title: Ask the comp question.
page.titleAccent: Get the answer on your data.
page.lede: Real prompts comp teams run in Pave Agent, the data each one draws on, and what comes back. Copy any prompt and run it in your own instance.
page.empty: No use cases match. Try a broader search.

cta.title: See it on your data
cta.text: We'll run this prompt in your Pave instance before we ever meet.

useCases.title: Answer a pay complaint with evidence
useCases.outcome: Go from "I think I'm underpaid" to a fact-based answer before the next 1:1.
useCases.problem: An employee says they're paid below market. You need to check their pay against the market, their band and their peers, then give their manager something to say.
oldWay: Export the employee and their peers from the HRIS
Look up the job in a benchmark survey and guess the match
Build a one-off spreadsheet, then write talking points from scratch
useCases.prompt: [Employee name] says they're paid below market. Compare their base and total cash to the market for their job, level and location, and to peers in the same role. Tell me whether the concern holds up, and draft talking points for their manager.
followUps: What would it cost to move them to our target percentile?
Is anyone else in this role in the same position?

yours.name: Employee record
yours.detail: Job, level, location, tenure and pay from your HRIS

pave.name: Market Pricing
pave.detail: Your priced job, matched to market

pave.name: Market Data benchmarks
pave.detail: Base and total cash by level and location

pave.name: Peer cohort
pave.detail: Companies like yours by size and industry

output.summary: The concern partly holds up. Base sits at the 38th percentile for a Senior Software Engineer in Denver, below your 50th percentile target. Total cash is at the 47th because of bonus. Two of five peers in the role are in the same position.

why.h: Your data and the market, together
why.p: Employee pay and live benchmarks sit in the same place. No exports, no lookups.
The comparison uses the job match your team already approved, so it's apples to apples.
If you target the 60th percentile for engineering, it measures against that, not a generic median.

useCases.title: Price a role you've never hired
useCases.outcome: Get a defensible range for a brand-new job by tomorrow, not next week.
useCases.problem: The business wants to open a role that isn't in your job architecture yet. The title is fuzzy, the hiring manager wants a number, and you need one you can defend.
oldWay: Search surveys for something close to the title
Argue about which level it maps to
Hand-build a range and hope it holds up in offers
useCases.prompt: We're opening a Staff Machine Learning Engineer role in Austin and remote US. Find the closest market matches, recommend a level in our architecture, and give me base, bonus and equity ranges at our target percentile.
followUps: How does this compare to our current IC5 engineering band?
What changes if we only hire in Austin?

yours.name: Adjacent bands
yours.detail: Ranges for similar roles you already have

pave.name: Equity benchmarks
pave.detail: Annual grant value by company stage

output.summary: Closest market match is Machine Learning Engineer at the Staff level. Recommended mapping is your IC5. Ranges below target your 60th percentile for Austin.

why.p: It reads the job description, not just the title, and shows you the match it picked.
The range lands in your architecture, so it fits next to the bands you already have.
Geo differentials come with the benchmark, not from a separate table.

useCases.title: Set a merit budget finance will sign
useCases.outcome: Show what each budget buys in market position, by department.
useCases.problem: Before the cycle, finance asks what budget you need. You need to show how far each team is from market and what different budgets get you.
oldWay: Pull current salaries and last cycle's increases
Age survey data forward by hand
Model three scenarios in a spreadsheet that breaks when anyone touches it
useCases.prompt: Model merit budgets of 3, 3.5 and 4 percent. For each, show the total cost and how many employees end up below the 25th percentile of market, by department. Recommend one.
followUps: What if engineering gets its own budget?
Show me the cost of a separate market adjustment pool instead.

pave.name: Market movement
pave.detail: How pay is trending for your jobs

output.summary: 3.5 percent keeps most employees at or above the 25th percentile at a cost of $4.2M. Engineering is the outlier and needs about 4.2 percent to hold its position.

why.h: Cycle and market in one model
why.p: Budget scenarios run on your real roster against current benchmarks.
Results roll up by your departments and managers, not generic job families.
Each figure links back to the employee and benchmark behind it.

useCases.title: Find top performers paid below market
useCases.outcome: A ranked list of who to fix first and what it costs.
useCases.problem: Your best people get recruited first. You want to find high performers below market before a competing offer does.
oldWay: Join a performance export with a pay export
Benchmark each role one by one
Send managers a spreadsheet they won't open
useCases.prompt: List employees rated "exceeds" or higher whose base is below the 40th percentile of market. Rank them by the cost to bring them to the 50th, and group by manager.
followUps: Which of these people were also passed over for a raise last cycle?
Draft a note to each manager with their list.

output.summary: 14 employees fit. Bringing all 14 to the 50th percentile costs $312,000. Six of them report to two managers in Product Engineering.

why.p: Ratings and market position are joined for you, across the whole company.
Ranked by cost and grouped by manager, so the next step is obvious.
Each list can go straight into Team View for the manager to see.

useCases.title: Pressure-test an offer before it goes out
useCases.outcome: Know if an offer will win and whether it breaks internal equity.
useCases.problem: A candidate has a competing offer. Recruiting wants to match. You need to know where the offer lands against market and against the people already in the role.
oldWay: Ask comp for a market check and wait
Look up current team pay separately
Decide under time pressure with half the picture
useCases.prompt: Our draft offer for a Senior Account Executive in New York is $140k base and $280k OTE. The candidate has a competing offer at $150k base. Where does our offer land against the market and our current team? What should we do?
followUps: What sign-on bonus closes the gap without changing base?
Update the offer letter with that structure.

yours.name: Current team pay
yours.detail: People in the same role and location

pave.name: Market Data benchmarks
pave.detail: Base and OTE for sales roles

pave.name: Peer cohort
pave.detail: Companies you compete with for talent

output.summary: Your draft is at the 55th percentile on base and the 62nd on OTE. Matching $150k base puts this hire above 4 of your 6 current Senior AEs in New York. Recommendation: hold base and add a $15k sign-on bonus.

why.h: Market and team in one answer
why.p: You see the competitive position and the equity risk side by side.
OTE and pay mix benchmarks, not just base.
The chosen structure flows into a Visual Offer Letter.

useCases.title: Spot equity refresh gaps
useCases.outcome: See who's about to hit a vesting cliff and what a refresh would cost.
useCases.problem: Initial grants are running out for your longest-tenured people. Their pay drops when vesting ends, and that's when they start taking recruiter calls.
oldWay: Pull vesting schedules from the cap table tool
Compare to refresh benchmarks by hand
Estimate share cost in a separate model
useCases.prompt: Which employees have less than 25 percent of their unvested equity value left over the next 12 months? Compare their ongoing equity to market refresh benchmarks and estimate the cost of bringing them to the 50th percentile.
followUps: What if we only refresh people rated "meets" or higher?

output.summary: 38 employees hit a vesting cliff in the next year. Their ongoing equity sits at the 22nd percentile of market refresh grants. Bringing them to the 50th costs about 0.4 percent of fully diluted shares.

why.p: It looks at what's left to vest, which is what actually drives retention.
Compares ongoing grants to ongoing grants, not to new-hire packages.
The same numbers show up in the employee's total rewards view.

useCases.title: Prep the comp committee summary
useCases.outcome: A one-page market position readout for the board, written in plain English.
useCases.problem: The comp committee meets next week. They want to know where you stand against market, where the gaps are, and what you plan to do about them.
oldWay: Rebuild last quarter's deck with new data
Hunt for the story in a dozen pivot tables
Rewrite it twice for tone
useCases.prompt: Summarize where we stand against the market by department and level for our comp committee. Highlight the three biggest gaps, what's driving them, and what we recommend. Keep it to one page.
followUps: Add how this changed since last quarter.

output.summary: Overall median position is the 52nd percentile against a 50th target. The three biggest gaps are Sales leadership, Data Science at mid levels, and Customer Success managers. All three trace to fast market movement since the last band refresh.

why.p: Plain language, ordered by what the committee cares about.
Your approved peer set is used every quarter, so trends are real.
Anyone can ask where a figure came from and get an answer.

useCases.title: Set pay for a new office location
useCases.outcome: Draft ranges for a city you've never hired in, in local currency.
useCases.problem: Leadership is opening an office in a new city. You need ranges for your most common jobs before recruiting starts posting roles.
oldWay: Buy or borrow a survey for that country
Map every job again
Convert currencies and sanity-check by hand
useCases.prompt: We're opening an office in Toronto. For our 12 most common jobs, show the market differential against our San Francisco ranges and draft Toronto ranges in CAD.
followUps: Which of these jobs have thin market data in Toronto?

yours.name: Headcount by job
yours.detail: To find your most common roles

output.summary: Toronto runs well below San Francisco for engineering and somewhat closer for go-to-market roles. Draft ranges below are in CAD at your 50th percentile target.

why.p: No extra survey to buy for a new country.
Ranges are drafted relative to what you already pay, so they fit your structure.
It tells you when a job has too little market data to trust.
